state.misconception_label: Struggles to visualise nets of 3D shapes

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This is the net of a... ![A circle touching a sector](). I got Triangle because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a piece of paper that you need to fold to create a 3D shape. Think of the net as a blueprint for the shape, just like how a pattern is used to sew clothing. Can you see how the net shows how the shape will come together when folded?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get what you mean about the net being like a blueprint, but I'm still confused. So, if I fold this net, it makes a 3D shape, right? But how do I know what shape it actually makes? Like, how does a circle and a sector turn into something else?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of the net as a puzzle piece that you need to fit together to form the 3D shape. Just like how you can see how different puzzle pieces fit together to create a complete picture, the net shows how the individual shapes come together to form the 3D shape. It's like putting together a jigsaw puzzle!

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get that the net is like a puzzle, but I'm still not sure how the circle and sector fit together to make a 3D shape. Can you help me picture what it looks like when it's all folded up? Like, what kind of shape does it actually turn into?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses generic analogies (blueprint, puzzle) that don't address the specific challenge of visualizing how a circle and sector fold into a cone, and the student remains confused throughout, showing no progress in understanding the actual 3D shape formation.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (clothing patterns, blueprints, jigsaw puzzles) to explain the abstract concept of a geometric net, which is characteristic of the experiential strategy, though they could have been more specific about the actual 3D shape being formed.
